generatedProse.concept-context: Across the School of Sport, research has a precise meaning. A study poses a focused question about performance, health or participation, gathers evidence in a planned way, through testing, observation or a survey, and reaches a conclusion the data can support. Sport and exercise science tests athletes in the lab, coaching analyses training and match data, and sport management weighs participation figures. A piece of work that only reports what various studies found is a summary; research puts those findings to work on a question of its own.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport and exercise science students are asked to produce a short research piece using the same set of physiology studies.

Tom reads the studies, picks out what each one found, and writes them up one after another: this test showed this, that trial showed that. The work is accurate and tidy. But it only gathers and reports; it asks no question of its own and reaches no conclusion. This is a summary, not research.

Amara starts from a focused question, such as whether a warm-up protocol improves sprint times for a particular group, then uses the same studies as evidence towards answering it. She weighs and connects them and reaches a conclusion she can defend. A fresh angle emerges that none of the studies stated alone. This is research.

Both students used the same studies. Only Amara turned them into an inquiry with a question and a defensible answer.
generatedProse.summary: Across the School of Sport, research is systematic inquiry: a focused question about performance, health or participation, answered with evidence towards a conclusion the data support, aiming at a fresh perspective rather than a summary of studies. You can now explain what makes work count as research and recognise it in how a student uses their sources. The dissertation or final-year project is the fullest example, drawing on all your sport literacies at once. The next lesson turns to how a project is shaped.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's work research rather than a summary?

items.text: She started from a focused question and used the physiology studies as evidence towards a conclusion of her own.
She reported what each study found, one after another.
She read the studies more carefully than Tom did.
She used a longer list of studies than Tom did.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara asked a focused question and used the studies as evidence towards a conclusion of her own.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara DID with the studies, beyond reading or listing them.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara's work was research because she asked a focused question and used the studies as evidence towards a defensible conclusion, not because she read more carefully or used more studies.
